nameStory: The brown-belted bumble bee gets its name from the distinctive brownish band that wraps around its fuzzy body like a belt. This earthy-colored stripe helps distinguish it from its many colorful cousins in the bumble bee family. The scientific name 'griseocollis' literally means 'gray neck,' referring to the grayish hairs often found on its thorax.
description: The brown-belted bumble bee is a robust, fuzzy pollinator about the size of your thumb. Like all bumble bees, it has a round, stocky body covered in dense, soft hair that makes it look like a flying teddy bear. Its most distinguishing feature is the brownish or rusty-colored band across its abdomen, contrasting with yellow and black stripes. These social bees live in underground colonies and are important native pollinators throughout most of the United States and southern Canada.

idTips.label: Brown Belt
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive brownish or rusty-orange band across the middle of the abdomen - this earthy stripe feels soft and velvety if you gently touch a deceased specimen

idTips.label: Body Size
idTips.description: Medium to large bumble bee, about thumb-sized, with a robust, rounded abdomen that appears plump and well-fed

idTips.label: Fuzzy Texture
idTips.description: Entire body covered in dense, soft hairs that feel like velvet - much fluffier than honey bees or wasps

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Flies with a characteristic loud, deep buzzing sound and somewhat clumsy, bouncing flight pattern between flowers

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Yellow and black stripes with the diagnostic brown belt, often with grayish hairs on the thorax (chest area)

habitat: Brown-belted bumble bees thrive in open areas with abundant flowers, including meadows, gardens, parks, and forest edges throughout New England. They prefer areas with diverse blooming plants from spring through fall and nest underground in abandoned rodent burrows or other cavities. You'll often spot them in suburban gardens, wildflower fields, and along hiking trails where native plants bloom.

seasonality.spring: Queens emerge from winter hibernation and begin establishing new colonies. Look for single, large individuals visiting early flowers like crocuses and fruit tree blossoms.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity with full colonies active. Workers are most abundant, busily visiting flowers throughout the day with their distinctive loud buzzing.
seasonality.fall: New queens and males emerge for mating. Activity gradually decreases as workers die off and only mated queens survive to hibernate.
seasonality.winter: Only fertilized queens survive, hibernating underground in leaf litter or soil until spring warmth awakens them.

funFact: Brown-belted bumble bees can 'buzz pollinate' by grabbing onto a flower and vibrating their flight muscles without moving their wings, creating vibrations so intense you can feel them through the flower stem - this technique releases pollen that other bees can't access!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other brown-marked bumble bees like the Red-belted Bumble Bee, but the Brown-belted has a more muted, earthy brown band rather than a bright rusty-red one. Memory trick: 'Brown-belted' sounds boring, and its brown is more subdued than its flashier red-belted cousin.
contextualKnowledge: With 16 different bumble bee species in New England, identification can be tricky since color patterns vary between queens, workers, and males of the same species. The Brown-belted Bumble Bee is one of the more widespread and stable species, unlike some of its rarer cousins that have declined significantly in recent decades.
compareHints: Among New England's bumble bees, the Brown-belted is most similar to the Red-belted Bumble Bee, but has a duller, more brownish belt versus bright rusty-red. It's larger and more robust than the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, which typically lacks the brown coloring entirely. The Half-black Bumble Bee might also cause confusion, but it has much more extensive black coloring on the abdomen.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's bumble bees, the Common Eastern Bumble Bee is distinguished by its predominantly black coloration with limited yellow banding, unlike the Brown-belted Bumble Bee which has brown fur, or the Tricolored Bumble Bee which sports distinctive white patches.
Among New England's many bumble bee species, the Two-spotted stands out for its clean black and yellow pattern with those diagnostic two spots.
The orange band is what sets the Tricolored Bumble Bee apart from its many relatives in New England.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, the Perplexing Bumble Bee has more white hairs on the head and distinctive reddish mandible tips.
Unlike the Common Eastern Bumble Bee which has more irregular yellow patches, the Yellow-banded has clean, complete yellow bands.

Northern Amber Bumble Bees stand out from other New England bumble bees by their uniform golden-yellow body combined with contrasting pale head hairs—most other species have distinct color bands or patterns.
Compared to the Common Eastern Bumble Bee, Half-black Bumble Bees are noticeably smaller and have more defined black banding rather than the Common Eastern's more blended yellow and black pattern.

Among New England's bumble bees, the Golden Northern stands out for its uniform golden-yellow coloration, while most relatives like the Common Eastern Bumble Bee have distinct black and white/yellow banding patterns.
Unlike social bumble bees in its genus, the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee lacks pollen baskets (specialized hairs for carrying pollen) since it doesn't need to provision its own nest.
Unlike other cuckoo bumble bees in New England like the Lemon Cuckoo Bumble Bee, the Yellowish Cuckoo has more muted, golden-yellow tones rather than bright lemon-yellow.
Red-belted bumble bees are much smaller than common eastern bumble bees and lack the solid yellow thorax of many other species.
